paras: The Pfeiffer Quarry spur camp shooting was an ambush in February 1903 in which unknown gunmen fired into the camp of a newly hired Black grading crew about seven miles north of Batesville, Arkansas. No one was reported hurt, but the ten or twelve workers abandoned the camp and fled to Batesville on their first night there. A Batesville paper headed its account "Inexcusable Lawlessness" while making light of the workers' flight.

W. H. Harris, chief contractor for grading the Pfeiffer Quarry spur, was said to have had "much trouble" securing and keeping enough men, although he paid "the best wage scale." Failing to get enough white men, he hired ten or twelve Black men on a Thursday and took them out to the quarry, where they set up camp to begin work the next day.

That Thursday night, soon after the camp was established, three shots were fired into it from a thicket. According to the Batesville Bee, the men were nervous but stayed, thinking "no real harm was intended." Then "a battery of guns opened up from the ambush," and the crew broke camp and, by their own account, were back in town within 15 minutes. A Pine Bluff report of 22 February put the flight "a day or two since," which places the shooting most likely on Thursday, 19 February.
Neither account identifies the gunmen beyond "unknown parties," and no report of arrests or an investigation was found.

The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic gave the episode two sentences on 22 February, attributing the shots to "unknown parties." The fuller account came from the Batesville Bee, reprinted in the Sharp County Record on 27 February under the headline "Inexcusable Lawlessness." Despite that heading, the item treated the workers' flight as a joke, quoting one of them in dialect on the "hundred guns" and remarking that "No train will ever make better time."
Neither paper suggested a motive, though the Bee set the attack directly after noting that Harris had turned to Black workers for want of white ones. No account in the Black press was found.

reader.title: Pfeiffer Quarry spur camp shooting
bases: Unknown gunmen fired into the camp of a newly hired Black grading crew, brought in after the contractor failed to get enough white men, and drove the crew off the job (A2, A3, A1).

The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic (A1) and the Batesville Bee item reprinted in the Sharp County Record (A2, A3) agree on shots fired into the Black laborers' camp near the Pfeiffer quarries and the workers' flight to Batesville, though both likely rest on Batesville reports.

accounts.label: Batesville Bee (reprinted)
accounts.gist: The contractor hired ten or twelve Black men when white labor was short; on their first night in camp three shots and then a volley from ambush drove them back to town within 15 minutes.

accounts.label: State news item
accounts.gist: Black laborers of the Pfeiffer quarries were frightened into leaving camp for Batesville after unknown parties fired shots into the camp.

framing.detail: The Sharp County Record ran the Bee's item under 'Inexcusable Lawlessness' but joked that 'No train will ever make better time' than the fleeing workers and rendered one in mock dialect.
The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic gave two flat sentences, calling the attackers 'unknown parties' and offering no motive or comment.
